newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK leader gives no word on future of local councils.
newsitem.headline: HK leader gives no word on future of local councils.

text.p: Hong Kong's future leader Tung Chee-hwa, who supports curbs on civil liberties, on Monday left the fate of elected local councillors in doubt after failing to guarantee their seats under Chinese rule.

Elected members of the Urban Council, Regional Council and District Boards, which play a major role in local government, have been fretting about their future after China's unveiling of plans in recent months to whittle down Hong Kong's fledgling democracy.

Tung's meeting with members of the Urban Council and District Boards on Monday was the latest in a series of negative signals on the future of human rights and democracy in Hong Kong after the British colony reverts to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30.
A week ago, the China-controlled Preparatory Committee, which is crafting Hong Kong's new political arrangements, approved a plan to replace the present local councils.
Tung, who co-chairs the Preparatory Committee, refused to promise that all incumbent local councillors would be allowed to serve beyond the mid-1997 handover to Beijing.
He said those who were allowed to serve would have to uphold the principle of "love China, love Hong Kong" and the Basic Law, the territory's post-colonial constitution.

"We all wish Hong Kong well ... we should unify to work for the good of Hong Kong's future, for the good of six million people. Therefore 'love China, love Hong Kong' and to uphold the Basic Law are the most basic considerations.
"People should not have any objection," Tung told reporters after meeting members of local councils.
However, he declined to say what constituted "love China, love Hong Kong" and whether pro-democracy councillors, who have vocally opposed China's policies, qualify.
Tung also dodged questions about whether councillors must back the controversial Provisional Legislature set up by a China-appointed body.
Democratic Party councillor Fred Li said he was dismayed that Tung had refused to directly answer questions about the future of pro-democracy members when he met them on Monday.
"He didn't particularly answer the question which those Democratic Party members asked ...," Li told reporters.

"Mr Tung always repeats the same old comment, that we need stability, we need a smooth transition, we don't want to see too many political disputes, arguments, in the Urban Council, in society as a whole."
Tung, who will replace British Governor Chris Patten, has lately echoed Beijing's tough line as Britain prepares to hand back the territory after more than 150 years of colonial rule.
He backs a Chinese plan to replace Hong Kong's elected Legislative Council with the shadow legislature and to repeal key clauses in the Bill of Rights.
The Democratic Party, the largest force in legislative elections in 1995, is excluded from the provisional legislature.

Under the proposals of the Preparatory Committee, Tung will expand membership of the local councils by 25 percent by appointing additional members. Serving members are expected to stay on but Tung will have the last word on who remains.
